segments.text: and you're just a brain, [[vat 0.15]] in a vat?
In 1641, René Descartes sat by his fire and asked what, if anything, he could know for certain.
He imagined an evil demon, [[demon]] as powerful as it was cunning, devoting all its energy to deceiving him. [[fool 0.4]] Every sight, every sound, even his own body, might be an illusion.
In 1981, Hilary Putnam brought the demon into the laboratory.
Imagine that an evil scientist has removed your brain, [[vat 0.2]] and placed it in a vat of nutrients that keeps it alive.
Its nerve endings are wired to a super-scientific computer, [[signals 0.1]] which feeds it exactly the signals a real body would.
You would see, hear and feel a perfectly normal world. [[same 0.4]] Everything would seem exactly as it does right now.
So how could you ever know that you're not a brain in a vat?

Here's why it matters. [[p1 0.5]] If you know you have hands, you know you're not a brain in a vat. [[p2 0.5]] But nothing you could ever experience would tell you that you're not. [[p3 0.5]] So, it seems, you don't know you have hands. [[all 0.6]] And the same goes for almost everything you believe.

Putnam's answer was surprising. [[causal 0.4]] Words, he argued, can only refer to things we are causally connected to. [[image 0.4]] A brain that has always lived in a vat has never met a real vat, only computer images of one. [[thought 0.4]] So when it thinks, “I am a brain in a vat,” it is talking about image-vats, and the thought is false. [[self 0.5]] So, Putnam concluded, we cannot be brains in vats.

Not everyone was convinced. [[recent 0.4]] The argument says nothing about a brain that was put in a vat only last night. Its words would still mean real vats. [[nagel 0.5]] And Thomas Nagel raised a stranger worry: perhaps we can't even think the truth of what we are, because we lack the concepts to do it.
So, could you ever know? And how?

This is the brain in a vat in its simplest form. Philosophers have since built many variations, [[sim]] like the idea that our entire universe might be a computer simulation. [[point 0.6]] The scenario is deliberately extreme. [[0.3]] Push doubt as far as it will go, and it shows us what we really mean when we say we know something.

publish.summary:
What if your brain had been removed from your body, kept alive in a vat of nutrients, and wired to a computer that feeds it a perfect simulation of the world? Everything would feel exactly as it does now. So how could you ever know that it isn't happening?

This short film traces the idea from René Descartes' evil demon (1641) to Hilary Putnam's brain in a vat (1981), sets out the skeptic's argument that threatens almost everything we believe, and walks through Putnam's surprising reply: that if we were brains in vats, we couldn't even truly think so. It ends with the objections that keep the debate alive.

discussion: Could you ever know you're not a brain in a vat? Leave your answer in the comments, along with your reasoning, especially if you can make the case for the other side.

Does Putnam's argument convince you, or does it just change the subject from knowledge to meaning? And is the brain in a vat even a valuable thought experiment, or too far-fetched to tell us anything?
Which thought experiment should we make next? Suggestions welcome.
